analysis.one_liner: Requires credit bureaus to give consumers free credit scores and lenders to disclose the scores they use before loans are signed.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 32–26 and printed it in November 2019, but the House never voted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require credit reporting agencies to give consumers a free credit score along with their free annual credit report, and to send free reports and scores automatically in situations like fraud alerts, disputes over errors, unemployment, or receiving public assistance. It would also require mortgage, auto, and private student lenders to show applicants — free of charge, before signing — the exact credit reports and scores used to judge them. Credit bureaus would have to explain how scores are calculated and warn buyers that the "educational" scores sold to consumers can differ from the scores lenders actually use.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers generally, and most of all people applying for a mortgage, car loan, or private student loan, who would see the exact scores and reports a lender used before signing. Low-income and unemployed consumers, fraud victims, and people disputing errors would get free reports and scores automatically instead of having to know the rules and ask. Anyone buying a credit score today would get it free with their annual report and would see how the score is built, what is holding it down, and how it compares with other consumers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Loan applicants and people checking their credit

how_it_helps.text: Consumers would get a free credit score with their free annual credit report, and free reports and scores automatically when they are unemployed and job hunting, on public assistance, are fraud victims, dispute an error, or place a fraud alert or security freeze — instead of paying for scores or hunting for the free-report rules.

Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders would have to give applicants, before they sign, the actual consumer reports and credit scores used to decide whether to extend credit — free of charge, with the lender barred from passing on the cost.

Score disclosures would have to explain what is helping and hurting the score (at least four factors of each), specific actions to improve it, the possible range, and a graph showing where the consumer stands compared with other consumers.

Credit bureaus would have to display prominent written warnings that there is no single credit score and that the 'educational' scores they sell to consumers may differ, sometimes substantially, from the scores lenders actually use — a confusion the Consumer Bureau found was widespread.

analysis.who_pays: Credit reporting agencies and credit score sellers lose the revenue they make charging consumers for scores and score-monitoring subscriptions, and must keep two years of past scores on file for consumer-only access. Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders take on new pre-signing disclosure duties and must absorb the cost of procuring the reports and scores.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus, score sellers, and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders would face new paperwork duties — delivering a separate disclosure document within three business days and before closing — and must pay the cost of obtaining the reports and scores themselves; 26 of the committee's members voted against even reporting the bill.

The bill is a disclosure fix, not a pricing or accuracy fix: outside the specific free circumstances it lists, credit bureaus could still charge consumers for scores and keep selling monitoring subscriptions, and the bill does nothing to correct errors in the underlying reports.

The added disclaimers and comparison charts add another layer of fine print to loan closings and score orders, which critics could argue burdens consumers with more paper without lowering the cost of credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and aimed at the exact moments people get hurt — signing a loan without knowing the score the lender used, or paying for a score that was available free. The costs are real but modest: compliance paperwork for lenders and lost score-sale revenue for the bureaus. The honest limitation is that the bill only patches disclosure; it leaves the bureaus' underlying fees and error-dispute machinery intact, so consumers still need separate remedies for inaccurate reports.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved and printed the bill in November 2019 and it went on the House's waiting list for floor votes, but House leaders never scheduled a vote before the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Joyce Beatty introduced the bill on July 5, 2019, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
The committee held a markup on July 11, 2019 and voted 32–26 to report the bill with amendments.

On November 21, 2019, the committee reported the amended bill (H. Rept. 116-306), Rep. Emanuel Cleaver signed on as an additional sponsor, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the House's holding list for bills awaiting a floor vote.
The bill drew only one cosponsor and never received a House floor vote; the record shows no further action after it was placed on the calendar.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired on the calendar without a vote, as happens to most bills that leadership never schedules.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and credit score sellers are better off, because they kept charging consumers for scores and monitoring subscriptions. Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders are better off because they never had to show applicants the scores they used before signing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and credit score sellers

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote was the committee's 32–26 approval to report the bill; the record does not break that vote down by party, the bill had just one cosponsor, and the House never voted at all.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion, and specialty bureaus)
industries.note: The bill cuts into their consumer-side business: a free score must come with every free annual report, reports and scores must be sent free after disputes, fraud alerts, or freezes, and the bureaus must post prominent warnings that the scores they sell may not match what lenders use. Their interest in charging consumers for scores runs directly against the bill's purpose.

The bill requires a score from a commonly used scoring model with rich explanatory disclosures, undercutting the market for paid consumer score products. Their lender-side score sales, which the findings show differ from what consumers see, continue untouched.

industries.industry: Mortgage, auto, and private student lenders
industries.note: They would have to hand applicants — before signing, and at the lender's expense — the exact reports and scores used in underwriting. That transparency helps borrowers shop and challenge rates, which is why lenders preferred the status quo.
